c0006: Average number of events you cater per year, counting every drop-off, buffet, wedding, party and live-fire booking. It is the main volume driver of the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, and years 2 and 3 grow in events. The example is a full-time pitmaster with a pit cook, not the average first year. Compare it with the capacity row further down.
c0008: EXCL. sales tax, with staffing and the service charge included and the voluntary gratuity left out: the blended price per guest across everything you sell, not the price of any one package. Price per guest incl. sales tax = this value × (1 + your sales tax rate). Operators quote by package (drop-off, staffed buffet, full-service); the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab shows the ranges. To bring a quote from the Pricing Calculator here, divide its subtotal plus the service charge you keep by the billable guests (its own price per guest excludes the service charge), then weight each package by the guests you expect to serve in a year.
c0010: Average number of guests per event across your whole mix, from drop-off lunches for a few dozen people to weddings of well over a hundred. Operators set guest minimums (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab). Sales per event = guests × price per guest. One cell for the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, so they always agree.
c0012: Growth in events in year 2 over year 1 (enter 0.12 for 12%). Kept conservative on purpose: reviews and wedding bookings build up months ahead, and a single smoker trailer limits how fast you can grow.
c0014: Growth in events in year 3 over year 2, kept conservative for the same reason: repeat corporate clients and planner referrals build up slowly, and one smoker trailer limits the weekends you can sell.
c0018: Share of sales that comes from BBQ packages: smoked meats, sides, bread and sauces, and the staffing that serves them. It is an INPUT: change it here and the P&L, the cash flow and the sales tax collected recalculate on their own. The rest of your sales are add-ons.
c0020: Calculated as the remainder: BBQ packages + add-ons = 100%. Add-ons are the live pit on site, desserts, appetizers, non-alcoholic drinks, rentals and travel fees.
c0022: Cost of goods sold on BBQ package sales: raw meat (bought at raw weight: brisket and pork butt yield about half after smoking), sides, bread and sauces, with a cushion for overproduction. The example sits inside the 28-35% food cost range for caterers in the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab. Meat prices swing, so it is the most sensitive lever in the plan: test it at the top of the range before you trust the result.
c0024: Cost of goods sold on add-ons: bought-in desserts and appetizers, and rentals you pass on at close to cost. The live pit on site is almost all margin. There is no alcohol in this line: the client buys it separately.
c0026: Disposables, wood and cooking fuel as a % of sales: plates, cutlery, napkins and foil pans, plus the wood, charcoal, pellets and propane backup that go into every cook (roughly 60-100 lb of wood per cook, or 27-45 kg: Kit estimate). It scales with the pounds of meat you smoke and the number of events. Vehicle and trailer fuel is NOT here: it has its own fixed line on the "3-Year P&L" tab. Some cities restrict foam and single-use plastics, so check your local rules.
c0032: Card and ACH fees on total sales. Private clients pay their deposit and balance by card; many companies pay by ACH or check, which lowers the cost. The example is a blended rate: a percentage plus a per-transaction fee, which weighs more on small invoices. Check your processor's statement and enter your effective rate (Kit estimate).
c0042: Monthly cost of your commissary kitchen (hours + storage) and the parking spot for your smoker trailer: one cell for everything you pay the commissary. Pick one where you can smoke in the yard, and ask the health department and the fire marshal before you sign. The deposit and the months before opening are calculated from it. Shared kitchens charge roughly 15-45 per hour (The Food Corridor, 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey): multiply by your cook hours and add storage and parking. A permitted commissary is required: smoked meat for clients cannot be cooked in a home kitchen, and cottage food rules do not cover it. Get quotes in your area before you sign.
c0046: Water, electricity and phone that the commissary fee does not cover. Wood, charcoal and propane backup are not here: they scale with your cooks and live in the disposables, wood and cooking fuel row above. It is the one cell for this cost, so you change it in one place and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0048: General liability or a BOP (venues and planners often require 1M per occurrence), commercial auto that covers the smoker trailer, workers' comp for your W-2 staff and inland marine for the smoker. Venues ask for a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as additional insured. Add liquor liability only if the client supplies alcohol and your staff serves it. Insureon publishes averages for small businesses (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab); the example is a Kit estimate, so get quotes from an insurance agent. It is counted once, as an annual expense, not also in startup costs.
c0050: Extra meat on the day, ice and parking at the venue: the unbudgeted costs of each event. It is a VARIABLE cost: it rises and falls with the number of events, so it cannot sit among the fixed costs or it would move the break-even without anyone noticing. Fuel is not here: vehicle and trailer fuel has its own fixed line on the "3-Year P&L" tab, and cooking fuel is in the disposables row.
c0055: Principal requested: bank or SBA 7(a). The example loan is above the $50,000 ceiling of the SBA Microloan, so it fits an SBA 7(a) loan or a secured bank loan. If your loan is an SBA 7(a), this is the cell. It is the only loan that the amortization schedule, the P&L interest and the DSCR use. The "Financing" tab checks that the sources of funds match the total cash needed on the "Startup Costs" tab (which includes working capital and the smoker trailer, van and fit-out contingency): copy the loan suggested there into this cell until the difference reaches zero. A lender will ask for your plan and projections.
c0057: Nominal annual rate (not APR). The example (10%) is the kit's assumption for an SBA 7(a) loan. A smaller loan secured by a smoker trailer, a used van and kitchen equipment often prices above a storefront loan: ask two lenders for quotes, and ask about SBA-guaranteed loans, before you set it.
c0059: Total years, interest-only period included. A smoker trailer and a van lose value faster than a storefront build-out, so the term is shorter. SBA 7(a) allows up to 10 years for equipment and working capital.
c0079: The smoker trailer, the van, their upfits (warming cabinet, storage boxes, racks, wrap) and the trailer inspection: everything mounted on a vehicle is depreciated with it. Straight-line book depreciation; tax methods such as MACRS or Section 179 are separate, so confirm with your accountant.
c0081: The live-fire rig, commissary storage fit-out, software, smallwares and pit tools, and holding and service equipment. Loading and unloading at every event wears them faster than a fixed kitchen, so a short life is prudent. Straight-line book depreciation; MACRS or Section 179 are tax treatments: confirm with your accountant.
c0087: INFORMATION ONLY: it does not enter any calculation in this workbook. It is your estimate of the most events a year your pit and crew can handle with one smoker trailer; Saturdays in May, June and October are the bottleneck. Compare it with the events per year you plan and with the optimistic scenario: if the plan goes above it, you need a second pit or more staff. Volume itself is driven by the "Events per year" cell above.
c0089: A new caterer does not book in month one what it books in month eight: weddings are reserved months ahead and corporate clients want to try you first. Events per year above is the year-1 AVERAGE: the ramp only spreads year 1's sales across the months (slower start, stronger finish) and keeps the annual total. At 100% there is no ramp.
c0093: Getting the commissary agreement, the permits, the fire inspection and the trailer ready takes weeks, and your test cooks happen before your first booking, so you pay commissary rent before you earn anything. It belongs in startup costs, not in the P&L.
c0095: Calculated by formula on the smoker trailer, its upfit, the van, its upfit and the trailer inspection lines: if you change the trailer price, the contingency recalculates on its own. The note on that row of the "Startup Costs" tab lists exactly which lines are included.
c0098: Average days between the event and the money in your bank. Private clients usually pay a 50% nonrefundable deposit when they book and the balance days before the event, and many companies pay at 30 days, so the example sits in between. Raise it if clients or marketplaces pay later. The workbook does not model deposits: they improve your real cash flow.
c0106: ZERO by default: a BBQ caterer sells no alcohol. If the client supplies it, a licensed service should pour it under its own insurance. Selling alcohol requires a liquor license (and, in some states, an event-by-event caterer's permit): check your state before adding it. Keep liquor liability coverage whenever your staff pours at your events.
c0144: A new offset or reverse-flow smoker trailer, 500-gallon class (wood, charcoal or pellets). Examples we read: Meadow Creek TS500 at $20,395 (webstaurantstore.com); Yoder Frontiersman at $8,495-$16,295 plus shipping (yodersmokers.com). The tow vehicle is YOUR pickup, at 0 in this plan. If you don't have one, budget a used pickup that tows at least 3,000 lb (1,360 kg): roughly 25,000-40,000 (Kit estimate).
c0147: Warming cabinet, hand sink and water tanks if your county requires them (smoking or serving at the event can make the trailer a mobile food unit), storage boxes and lights.
c0149: Live-fire rig for the premium line: Santa Maria grill, Argentine parrilla, asado crosses and La Caja China for pig roasts. It is depreciated with the equipment. Lower it to 0 if you will only smoke.
c0151: Racks, meat lugs and a vacuum sealer in the commissary. Ask the kitchen what it already provides before you budget this line.
c0153: A used cargo van for drop-offs and buffets: it carries the hot boxes and insulated food carriers. It is not refrigerated: cooked meat travels in hot holding at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, and raw meat goes from your supplier to the commissary. Prices vary with size, mileage and condition, so get several quotes. A Transit-size van does not need a CDL (that starts at 26,001 lb GVWR).
c0155: Shelving, racks, tie-downs for hot boxes and carriers, and the vehicle wrap.
c0157: State filing fees for the LLC (Secretary of State) plus an attorney's review of your standard contract (50% nonrefundable deposit, cancellation tiers and a burn ban clause) or a filing service; a registered agent is also needed. Fees vary a lot by state. The "Taxable / recoverable tax?" column is set to No: it only matters if you enter a recoverable input tax rate (for example UK VAT).
c0160: Varies a lot by city, county and state: get the amounts for yours before you close the budget. Expect the catering or health permit, mobile food unit or temporary event permits, the fire marshal inspection, the business license, the sales tax permit, ServSafe Manager and food handler cards.
c0162: Only if your county requires it: some review the trailer or your written procedures before issuing the permit and charge a plan review fee. In Texas, a mobile food unit works out of a central preparation facility (25 TAC §228.221). If your county doesn't, enter 0.
c0164: Catering software for proposals, e-signature contracts, deposits and final balances, plus a card reader and a tablet.
c0166: Knives, cutting boards, hotel pans, calibrated probe thermometers, butcher paper and foil, and heat-resistant gloves: the tools that get depreciated. Daily disposables are NOT depreciated: they go in the disposables, wood and cooking fuel line of the P&L, at the % of sales set in the "0. Assumptions" tab.
c0168: Meat for your test cooks, rubs, sauces, wood and disposables for your first events. With 0% recoverable input tax (the US default), any sales tax you pay on this purchase is treated as a cost.
c0170: Website, photos of the meat and the smoker trailer, listings on The Knot, WeddingWire, Zola and ezCater, Google Business Profile and your first bridal show.
c0172: Six insulated food carriers, two hot boxes, ten chafing dishes, coolers, tables, a canopy and a cutting board for the carving station.
c0180: What you buy: smoker trailer, van, upfits, live-fire rig, equipment, launch and formation costs. The cash cushion is not an investment: it is working capital.
c0205: Sales of BBQ packages: the smoked meats, sides, bread and sauces plus the staffing that serves them, across drop-offs, buffets, parties, weddings and live-fire events. All of it carries cost of goods sold at the BBQ package rate.
c0207: Sales of add-ons: the live pit on site (your smoker trailer at the event, a paid extra), desserts, appetizers, non-alcoholic drinks, rentals and travel fees. The client buys any alcohol separately, so there is no alcohol revenue.
c0221: The monthly amount is typed in "0. Assumptions"; here it is multiplied by twelve. It covers your commissary hours, storage and the parking spot for the smoker trailer, not storefront rent. The months before opening are on the "Startup Costs" tab and are NOT counted twice.
c0225: Water, electricity and phone that the commissary fee does not cover. No propane or wood here: they scale with your cooks and sit in the disposables, wood and cooking fuel line.
c0235: Licensed hauler for trash, grease and ash. Ask the commissary first: many include pickup in the fee. If yours does not, get a quote in your area. Let ash cool completely and keep it in a metal container with a lid.
c0237: Repairs for the smoker and your equipment: doors, gaskets, thermometers, and the wheels and lights of the trailer.
c0239: ServSafe Manager (Certified Food Protection Manager) and food handler cards for you and your team, plus their renewals. The required cards vary by state.
c0241: Food cost and labor for the tastings you offer couples, planners and companies (meat, sides and pit hours). Many caterers charge a fee and credit it toward the booking: if you do, lower this line.
c0265: Floor set by this workbook: kit benchmark (editable estimate). The workbook's gross margin also subtracts card fees, marketplace commissions and miscellaneous costs, so the floor sits below the 65-70% that caterer pricing guides quote on food cost alone.
c0268: Ceiling for cost of goods (disposables, wood and cooking fuel have their own line): kit benchmark (editable estimate), based on the 28-35% food cost range for caterers in the benchmarks table.
c0270: Ceiling: kit benchmark (editable estimate), above the 25-35% labor range that pricing guides report because it includes the owner/pitmaster's own pay.
c0272: There is no storefront rent in this workbook: 7% is a prudent ceiling for the commissary kitchen and smoker trailer parking, a kit benchmark (editable estimate). A business with its own fixed kitchen carries a much higher occupancy cost.
c0344: Sells, runs the tastings, plans menus, and works the pit and the carving station at weddings and premium events. Covers the main shift at every event. The rest of the owner's pay comes from profit.
c0346: Pit cook / lead cook, part-time W-2: runs the overnight cook with probes and handles hot holding. One pit cook can watch several cooks at once. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE, around the 75th percentile for restaurant cooks (BLS OEWS, May 2025).
c0348: Servers, buffet attendants and carvers hired per event and paid hourly as W-2 employees, about one per 25-30 guests at a buffet (Kit estimate). Their FTE is a fraction because they only work event hours. Treating them as 1099 contractors is a misclassification risk (FLSA; California AB5). Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE. The voluntary gratuity is theirs.
c0350: Part-time W-2 prep cook and driver: portions and mixes rubs in the commissary, loads the van and drives to venues. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0364: Hours of work per person for one event: portioning, the overnight cook, loading, travel, setup, two to three hours of service, breakdown and cleanup. Serving is only part of it. Hours × people × events per year sets the event staff cost.
c0366: Average number of people working each event: about 1.5 on a drop-off, 3 on a staffed buffet, 4 on a full-service company event, 5 at a wedding and 4 on a live-fire booking (Kit estimate). Raise it for bigger events: the staffing sizes itself.
c0379: 1. "0. Assumptions" is the control sheet: events per year, price per guest excl. sales tax, guests per event, the mix of BBQ packages and add-ons, cost of goods sold, commissary and smoker trailer parking, financing and taxes.
c0419: Commissary kitchen and smoker trailer parking
c0421: A monthly commissary cost (hours + storage) and the parking spot for the smoker trailer, plus a deposit and rent for the months before opening
c0429: Two useful lives: the smoker trailer, the van and their upfits on one, and the live-fire rig and the equipment on the other. The Startup Costs tab calculates the annual charge.
c0430: The trailer and the van wear out at a different speed than the rig and the equipment. Working capital, opening inventory and launch marketing are not fixed assets, so they are not depreciated.
c0431: Smoker trailer and van insurance, and liability
c0441: A percentage calculated on the smoker trailer, van and upfit lines
c0442: If you change the trailer price, the contingency recalculates instead of staying at the old amount.
c0460: A miscellaneous line typed in among the fixed costs
c0462: Extra meat, ice and venue parking rise and fall with the number of events: among the fixed costs they would distort the break-even.
c0476: Price per person by service type
c0479: A Kansas City operator in 2023 quoted drop-off from $17.50 per person. The example in this workbook blends drop-off, party, corporate, wedding and live-fire events, so its price per guest sits between the two ends.
c0483: 30-guest minimum and an event fee of $1,000-$1,200. Prices differ a lot by market: collect three local quotes before you set yours.
c0487: Cooked weight: 6-8 oz with two or three meats; a floor of 1/4-1/3 lb when there are many sides. The Pricing Calculator buys by raw pounds.
c0491: Average for caterers. A new business with a loan to repay starts lower: improve it with more events, bigger events or a higher price per guest.
c0495: Brisket and pork butt lose about half their weight in the smoker: 300 guests need roughly 200 lb (91 kg) of raw meat. Buy and cost by raw weight.
c0499: Caterer food cost as a share of the price. Meat prices swing, so re-cost every quote and test the result at the top of the range.
c0503: Offset smokers on a trailer: Yoder Frontiersman at $8,495, $11,295 and $16,295 plus shipping; Meadow Creek TS500 (500-gallon class) at $20,395. Your tow vehicle is extra.
c0507: ezCater lists about 15% on food and delivery, plus card processing. Fees change: check the current schedule before you count on a rate.
c0511: Common at booking to hold the date. The balance is due about 72 hours before a party or up to 14 days before a wedding; companies often pay at 30 days. The workbook does not model deposits, so they improve your real cash flow.
c0515: Median hourly wages for restaurant cooks (35-2014), nonrestaurant food servers (35-3041) and chefs and head cooks (35-1011); 75th percentile $21.45 for cooks and $18.51 for servers. The plan pays the pit cook near the 75th percentile and the owner/pitmaster below the chefs and head cooks median: the rest comes from profit.
c0519: 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey; 42% of operators charge $20-$29 per hour. Storage and parking cost extra, and not every kitchen lets you smoke in the yard.
c0523: 30 guests at one operator; 75 for full catering and 20 for delivery at another; food from $28 per person with a $500 minimum at a third. Set yours by service style.
c0527: Insureon averages for businesses under 5 employees: general liability, BOP, workers' comp and commercial auto. Your quotes will differ; add liquor liability only if your staff pours the client's alcohol.
c0529: 60-100 lb (27-45 kg) of wood per cook · 1 server per 25-30 guests
c0531: Wood use varies with the smoker, the weather and the fuel. A buffet needs about one server per 25-30 guests; one pit cook can watch several cooks at once.
c0597: The same calculation on what you BUY (smoker trailer, van, upfits, live-fire rig, equipment, launch and formation costs), without working capital: that money is not spent, it is tied up and comes back when the business closes. For reference only: the payback that matters is the one above
